questions.stem: Whose X-ray diffraction work produced ‘Photo 51’, the image that gave key evidence that DNA is a helix?
options: Erwin Chargaff
Rosalind Franklin
James Watson
Francis Crick
questions.explanation: Photo 51 was taken in 1952 in Rosalind Franklin’s laboratory at King’s College London, with her student Raymond Gosling. Watson and Crick built their 1953 model partly from this evidence, which Maurice Wilkins showed to Watson early in 1953. Chargaff contributed base-ratio data, not X-ray images.

questions.stem: Erwin Chargaff found that in DNA from many species, the amount of adenine always equals the amount of thymine, and guanine equals cytosine. How did this help Watson and Crick?
options: It proved that DNA, rather than protein, is what carries the genes
It showed that every species has exactly the same sequence of DNA bases
It suggested that A pairs with T and G pairs with C across the helix
It showed that a DNA molecule is made of one single, unpaired strand
questions.explanation: Equal amounts of A and T, and of G and C, are exactly what you would expect if the bases pair up across two strands, which became the rungs of the double helix. Paired bases imply two strands, not one. Chargaff’s ratios also differ between species in their overall proportions of A–T to G–C, so they do not show that all DNA is the same.

questions.stem: A sample of DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases is guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 30%, making 60% A and T together. The remaining 40% is shared equally between guanine and cytosine, so guanine is 20%. The answer 40% is guanine and cytosine combined, and 30% wrongly pairs guanine with adenine.

questions.stem: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published a model of the structure of DNA. What did it show?
options: A flat ladder of bases with no twist at all
A double helix with paired bases in the middle
A single helix with the bases on the outside
A triple helix with the phosphates at the centre
questions.explanation: The Watson–Crick model has two sugar–phosphate backbones twisted into a double helix, with the bases paired A–T and G–C on the inside. A triple helix with phosphates at the centre was a rival model proposed by Linus Pauling earlier that year, and it was wrong. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize; Franklin had died in 1958 and could not be included.

questions.stem: What is a genome?
options: The complete set of genetic material in an organism
A single section of DNA that codes for one protein
One tightly coiled molecule of DNA wound around proteins
The pair of alleles that an organism has for one trait
questions.explanation: A genome is all of an organism’s DNA, including every gene on every chromosome. A section of DNA that codes for one protein is a gene, and a coiled DNA molecule wound around proteins is a chromosome. From smallest to largest: gene, chromosome, genome.

questions.stem: In a classroom DNA extraction from mashed strawberries, what is the detergent for?
options: It makes the DNA come out of solution so that it can be seen
It cuts the DNA into single genes so they can be identified
It stains the DNA a bright colour so that it shows up in the tube
It breaks down cell and nuclear membranes to release the DNA
questions.explanation: Membranes are made of fats, and detergent breaks them apart just as it breaks up grease on dishes, letting the DNA spill out of the nucleus. Salt then helps the DNA strands clump together. The DNA becomes visible only at the end, when ice-cold ethanol is poured on top and the DNA comes out of solution as white strands.

questions.stem: Australian merino sheep were bred over many generations from the animals with the finest, heaviest fleeces. What is this process called?
options: Selective breeding
Genetic engineering
Natural selection
Cloning
questions.explanation: Choosing which animals breed so that a desired trait becomes more common is selective breeding, also called artificial selection. It works with the variation already present and does not insert genes from another species, as genetic engineering does. In natural selection the environment, not people, decides which individuals reproduce.

questions.stem: A farmer plants a wheat variety in which every plant is genetically almost identical, because it was bred for high yield. What is the main risk?
options: The high yield will stop the plants from forming any new seeds
A single new disease could infect and kill nearly every plant
The plants will start to mutate faster than a mixed crop would
The plants will cross-pollinate and turn back into wild grasses
questions.explanation: With so little genetic variation, if one plant has no resistance to a new disease, almost none of the others do either. A varied population is more likely to include some individuals that survive. Selective breeding narrows the gene pool; it does not make plants mutate faster.

questions.stem: What is a transgenic organism?
options: An organism containing a gene from a different species
An organism produced by mating two different breeds together
An organism that is an exact genetic copy of another
An organism whose genes were changed by radiation
questions.explanation: Transgenic organisms are made by genetic engineering, which moves a gene from one species into another. Mating two breeds of the same species is ordinary breeding, and an exact genetic copy is a clone. Radiation can cause random mutations, but it does not add genes from another species.

questions.stem: Since the 1980s, most insulin for people with diabetes has been made by genetically modified microorganisms. How was this made possible?
options: Bacteria were fed human insulin, which they learnt to copy
Bacteria naturally make insulin identical to human insulin
The human insulin gene was inserted into bacterial plasmids
Bacteria were selectively bred to make more of their insulin
questions.explanation: Scientists cut the human insulin gene out with restriction enzymes and joined it into plasmids, small rings of bacterial DNA, which the bacteria then copy and use to make human insulin. Bacteria do not make insulin naturally, so selective breeding had nothing to work with. Before this, insulin was extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle.

questions.stem: In genetic engineering, what is the job of a restriction enzyme?
options: To carry the new gene into the host cell
To cut DNA at a specific sequence of bases
To join two pieces of DNA together permanently
To make many copies of a short piece of DNA
questions.explanation: Each restriction enzyme recognises a particular short base sequence and cuts the DNA there, so the same enzyme can cut out a gene and open up a plasmid to receive it. Joining the pieces together is done by a different enzyme, DNA ligase. Carrying the gene into the cell is the job of a vector such as a plasmid.

questions.stem: Most cotton grown in Australia is Bt cotton, which carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. What does this gene do for the plant?
options: It lets the plant grow with no water during a drought
It makes the cotton fibre grow in a range of colours
It makes the plant resistant to every type of weedkiller
It makes a protein that kills certain caterpillar pests
questions.explanation: The Bt gene codes for a protein that is toxic to the caterpillars that feed on cotton, so farmers need far less insecticide spray. Some cotton varieties also carry a separate gene for tolerance to one particular herbicide, but no gene makes a plant resistant to every weedkiller. Bt cotton still needs irrigation or rain like any other cotton crop.

questions.stem: Golden rice has been genetically engineered to help address which problem?
options: Insect pests that eat rice plants in the field
Rice crops dying when salt water floods the paddies
Vitamin A deficiency in people who rely on rice
Iron deficiency in people who eat little meat
questions.explanation: Golden rice carries genes that make the grain produce beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A, and the beta-carotene gives the rice its golden colour. Vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and weakens the immune system, especially in children. The other problems are real, but they are not what golden rice was designed to solve.

questions.stem: What does the CRISPR-Cas9 technique allow scientists to do?
options: Read the complete genome sequence of an organism
Join two eggs together to form an embryo
Cut and edit DNA at a precise, chosen location
Make an exact copy of a whole adult animal
questions.explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 uses a short guide RNA to lead the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence, where it cuts so that a gene can be removed, disabled or corrected. Making a copy of a whole animal is cloning, and reading a genome is sequencing, which are different technologies. CRISPR is being trialled as a form of gene therapy for disorders such as sickle-cell anaemia.

questions.stem: What is the aim of gene therapy?
options: To produce a baby that is a genetic copy of one of its two parents
To find out whether a person carries an allele for a genetic disorder
To treat a genetic disorder by correcting faulty genes in body cells
To prevent an infection by injecting a weakened form of the pathogen
questions.explanation: Gene therapy adds a working copy of a gene, or repairs a faulty one, in a patient’s cells so that the disorder improves. Injecting a weakened pathogen is vaccination. Finding out whether someone carries an allele is genetic testing, which identifies a problem but does not treat it.

questions.stem: Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was cloned by placing the nucleus of an udder cell from one sheep into an egg cell from a second sheep, which then grew inside a third sheep. Whose chromosomes did Dolly carry?
options: An equal mix from all three of the sheep
The sheep that donated the udder cell
The sheep that donated the egg cell
The sheep that gave birth to Dolly
questions.explanation: The egg’s own nucleus was removed, so all of Dolly’s chromosomes came from the udder-cell nucleus, making her a clone of that sheep. The surrogate mother provided a uterus to grow in but no DNA. Plant cuttings and tissue culture are much older and simpler ways of producing clones.

questions.stem: What makes embryonic stem cells especially useful in medical research?
options: They contain no DNA, so the body never rejects them
They can develop into almost any type of body cell
They have already specialised into one type of cell
They divide by meiosis to make new gametes for IVF
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, meaning they can become almost any cell type, so they may one day replace damaged tissue such as heart muscle or nerve cells. Adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, are more limited and usually make only a few related cell types. Using embryos raises ethical questions that adult stem cells avoid.

questions.stem: The HeLa cell line, used in medical research around the world since the 1950s, grew from cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks. What is the main ethical issue in her case?
options: Her cells were sold back to her family to be used in her treatment
Her cells were taken and used without her knowledge or consent
Her cells were used to clone a person who was genetically her
Her cells were genetically modified so that they caused cancer
questions.explanation: In 1951 doctors kept a sample of Henrietta Lacks’s tumour without asking her, and for decades neither she nor her family knew her cells were being grown and sold for research. HeLa cells helped develop the polio vaccine and many other advances, which makes the case a classic example of research benefit versus consent. Today, researchers must get informed consent before using a person’s tissue.

questions.stem: In a paternity test, how does a DNA profile show who a child’s biological father is?
options: Every band in the child’s profile is also found in the man’s profile
Every band not inherited from the mother appears in the man’s profile
The child’s whole DNA profile is identical, band for band, to the father’s
The child’s profile shares no bands at all with the mother’s profile
questions.explanation: A child inherits half of their DNA from each parent, so each band in the profile must come from either the mother or the father; any band not found in the mother must match the biological father. A child’s profile is not identical to either parent’s, because it is half from each. Matching every band to the man would also mean the mother contributed nothing.

questions.stem: A genetic test shows that a person carries an allele that greatly raises their risk of a disease later in life. Which of these is an ethical question rather than a scientific one?
options: On which chromosome is the allele for this disease located?
Should insurers or employers be allowed to see the result?
How accurately does the test detect this particular allele?
Which protein does this allele code for in the body’s cells?
questions.explanation: Scientific questions can be answered by evidence and experiment, while ethical questions are about what people ought to do. Whether insurers or employers should see the result involves privacy and fairness, and no experiment can settle it. The accuracy of the test, the protein made and the chromosome involved can all be measured or observed.
